subsections: Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings
Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with reference to the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
o: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar — Co-author of the Munshi-Ayyangar language formula
Syed Mohammad Saadullah — Representative from Bombay
N. Madhava Rao — Original member in place of B.L. Mitter
T.T. Krishnamachari — Replaced Dr. K.M. Munshi
accepted.x: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar was associated with the Munshi-Ayyangar language formula. Saadullah was from Assam, Madhava Rao replaced B.L. Mitter, and T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure member–role pair and eliminate swapped replacements and locations.
accepted.sec: ■ Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
With reference to the Drafting Committee, consider the following statements:
1. Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a jurist.
2. Dr. K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee.
3. Dr. K.M. Munshi was originally the only Congress member of the Drafting Committee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a jurist, while K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee and was originally the only Congress member of the Drafting Committee.
accepted.tq: Check each member–description pair separately before selecting the coded combination.
accepted.sec: ■ Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following statements about the Draft Constitution is correct?
o: It was published in February 1948 with 315 Articles and 13 Schedules.
It was published in February 1949 with 395 Articles and 8 Schedules.
It was published in November 1948 with 299 Articles and 13 Schedules.
It was published in October 1947 with 315 Articles and 12 Schedules.
accepted.x: The Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948 and contained 315 Articles and 13 Schedules.
accepted.tq: Separate the publication date from the final Constitution’s later article and schedule figures.
accepted.sec: ■ Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Drafting Committee completed its draft in less than six months after sitting for approximately how many days?
accepted.x: The Drafting Committee sat for only 141 days and completed its draft in under six months.
accepted.tq: Use the distinctive numerical figure as the anchor and reject nearby invented values.
accepted.sec: ■ Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The initial draft prepared by B.N. Rau in October 1947 was primarily based on:
o: The Government of India Act, 1919 alone
The recommendations of the International Court of Justice
The resolutions of the Indian National Congress alone
The reports of the Constituent Assembly committees
accepted.x: B.N. Rau’s initial draft of October 1947 was built on the reports of the Constituent Assembly committees.
accepted.tq: Identify the stated institutional source instead of choosing a familiar but over-exclusive constitutional source.
accepted.sec: ■ Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Office-bearer)
(a) Temporary President of the Constituent Assembly
(b) Permanent President of the Constituent Assembly
(c) Constitutional Adviser
(d) Speaker when sitting as Dominion Legislature

List-II (Person)
(i) B.N. Rau
(ii) G.V. Mavalankar
(iii) Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
(iv) Dr. Rajendra Prasad

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President, Rajendra Prasad the permanent President, B.N. Rau the Constitutional Adviser and G.V. Mavalankar the Dominion Legislature Speaker.
accepted.tq: Start with the distinctive temporary President and Dominion Legislature Speaker pairs.

accepted.s: Who was elected as the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly at its first sitting on 9 December 1946?
accepted.x: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the eldest member, served as the temporary President at the first sitting on 9 December 1946.
accepted.tq: Link the first sitting and the temporary office before considering the permanent office.

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the office-bearers of the Constituent Assembly:
1. Dr. Rajendra Prasad became its permanent President from 11 December 1946.
2. H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari were its Vice-Presidents.
3. B.N. Rau later became a judge of the International Court of Justice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. Rajendra Prasad became permanent President from 11 December 1946, Mukherjee and Krishnamachari were Vice-Presidents, and B.N. Rau later served as an International Court of Justice judge.
accepted.tq: Verify the dates, paired office-holders and later career detail independently.

accepted.s: G.V. Mavalankar served as the Speaker when the Constituent Assembly sat as the Dominion Legislature from:
accepted.x: G.V. Mavalankar became Speaker when the Constituent Assembly was functioning as the Dominion Legislature on 17 November 1947.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the Dominion Legislature office from the Constituent Assembly’s earlier presidential appointments.

accepted.s: Before Partition, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was elected to the Constituent Assembly from:
o: United Provinces, with the support of B.N. Rau
Assam, with the support of Syed Mohammad Saadullah
Bombay, with the support of M.R. Jayakar
Bengal, from the Jessore-Khulna area, with the support of Jogendra Nath Mandal
accepted.x: Before Partition, Ambedkar was elected from Bengal’s Jessore-Khulna area with the support of Jogendra Nath Mandal.
accepted.tq: Separate the pre-Partition constituency from the later Bombay constituency.

accepted.s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar lose his Constituent Assembly seat after Partition?
o: He resigned from the Assembly before the Constitution was drafted.
The Jessore-Khulna districts went to East Pakistan.
The Bombay seat was abolished by the Constituent Assembly.
He was disqualified from contesting elections.
accepted.x: The Jessore-Khulna districts, from which Ambedkar had been elected, went to East Pakistan after Partition, causing him to lose that seat.
accepted.tq: Trace the political consequence of territorial reorganisation rather than confusing it with resignation or disqualification.

accepted.s: After Partition, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was re-elected to the Constituent Assembly from Bombay in the seat vacated by:
accepted.x: Ambedkar was re-elected from Bombay in 1947 to the seat vacated by M.R. Jayakar.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a constituency vacancy from the Drafting Committee’s member replacements.

accepted.s: In response to the criticism that the Constitution borrowed substantially from the Government of India Act, 1935, Ambedkar argued that:
o: The Constitution had copied the Act without any alteration.
The Government of India Act, 1935 had no useful provisions.
Borrowing tested provisions was no shame and required no apology.
Only the Constituent Assembly committees were responsible for the borrowing.
accepted.x: In his speech of 4 November 1948, Ambedkar defended the adaptation of tested provisions and said that there was no need to apologise for such borrowing.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise nature of a constitutional defence instead of accepting the extreme claim of wholesale copying.

accepted.s: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described which provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
accepted.x: Article 32, which guarantees the Right to Constitutional Remedies, was described by Ambedkar as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution.
accepted.tq: Match the famous phrase with the constitutional provision, not with the related social-justice articles.

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Ambedkar’s conception of federalism:
1. India was described as a Union of States.
2. The Union was considered indestructible.
3. The States were recognised as having a constitutional right to secede.
4. The system could work as unitary or federal according to circumstances.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Ambedkar’s conception did not recognise a right of the States to secede from the Union.
accepted.tq: Spot the reversed federal principle in the statement asserting a right to secede.

accepted.s: Ambedkar favoured a strong Centre primarily to:
o: Replace Fundamental Rights with Directive Principles
Permit States to withdraw from the Union
accepted.x: Ambedkar favoured a strong Centre as a means of protecting weaker sections while retaining a constitutional system capable of functioning in federal or unitary conditions.
accepted.tq: Link the institutional preference to its stated social-justice objective.

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 32 — Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Article 356 — Equal opportunity in public employment
accepted.x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice punishable. Article 32 concerns constitutional remedies, Article 46 concerns SC/ST welfare, and Article 356 concerns emergency provisions in States.
accepted.tq: Use article-number discrimination and reject familiar provisions assigned to the wrong article.

accepted.s:
Which of the following combinations correctly represents constitutional measures associated with Ambedkar’s interventions for equality and representation?
1. Articles 15 and 16 — Non-discrimination and equal opportunity
2. Article 46 — Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
3. Articles 330 and 332 — Reserved seats
4. Universal adult suffrage including women from the beginning
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: All four statements are correct. The constitutional framework combined equality provisions, welfare directions, reserved representation and universal adult suffrage including women from the outset.
accepted.tq: Group the related equality provisions and test whether any one has been improperly excluded.

accepted.s: Ambedkar regarded the Directive Principles of State Policy as:
o: Applicable only during a national emergency
Unrelated to social and economic justice
Superior to all Fundamental Rights in judicial enforcement
Equally important for social and economic justice and a novel feature like instruments of instructions
accepted.x: Ambedkar considered the Directive Principles equally important for social and economic justice and described them as a novel feature resembling instruments of instructions.
accepted.tq: Choose the complete conceptual description rather than an extreme claim of judicial superiority.

accepted.s: Ambedkar hoped that the emergency provisions under Article 356 would remain a:
o: Source of the Union’s power to secede
accepted.x: Ambedkar expressed the hope that Article 356 would remain a ‘dead letter’, indicating that it would not be used routinely.
accepted.tq: Match the distinctive quotation with the correct emergency provision.

accepted.s: Which statement best reflects Ambedkar’s position on the Uniform Civil Code?
o: It should be rejected as incompatible with the Constitution.
It should be imposed immediately on every community without exception.
It could be voluntary and apply to those who declared themselves willing.
It could operate only during an emergency.
accepted.x: Ambedkar advocated a Uniform Civil Code but suggested that it could initially be voluntary, applying to persons who declared themselves willing to be governed by it.
accepted.tq: Distinguish advocacy of a principle from the proposed voluntary method of application.

accepted.s: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar delivered his final speech in the Constituent Assembly on:
accepted.x: Ambedkar delivered his final speech in the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949.
accepted.tq: Separate the final speech date from Constitution Day and the date of commencement of the Constitution.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: Which of the following was NOT one of the three warnings given by Ambedkar in his final Constituent Assembly speech?
o: Turn political democracy into social democracy.
Abolish the parliamentary system in favour of a presidential system.
Give up the bloody methods of revolution and civil disobedience.
Do not lay liberties at the feet of a great man.
accepted.x: Ambedkar warned against violent and extra-constitutional methods, hero-worship in politics, and the failure to establish social democracy. He did not call for abolishing the parliamentary system.
accepted.tq: Find the option outside the recognised set of three warnings.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: Ambedkar used the expression ‘the grammar of anarchy’ while warning against:
o: The principle of universal adult suffrage
Bloody methods of revolution and civil disobedience after constitutional methods became available
accepted.x: ‘The grammar of anarchy’ referred to the continued use of bloody revolutionary methods and civil disobedience when constitutional methods were available.
accepted.tq: Connect the memorable phrase with the specific conduct criticised in the speech.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: According to Ambedkar’s warning about bhakti or hero-worship in politics, excessive devotion to a great leader could lead to:
accepted.x: Ambedkar warned that placing liberties at the feet of a great man, or political hero-worship, could lead to dictatorship.
accepted.tq: Trace the stated political consequence of excessive personal devotion.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: Ambedkar’s reference to India entering ‘a life of contradictions’ on 26 January 1950 pointed to the coexistence of:
o: Federalism with the right of secession
Political equality with social and economic inequality
accepted.x: The contradiction lay in political equality coexisting with inequality in social and economic life. Ambedkar urged that political democracy be transformed into social democracy.
accepted.tq: Match each side of the contrast without reversing the domains of equality and inequality.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s:
With reference to constitutional morality, consider the following statements:
1. Ambedkar borrowed the term from George Grote.
2. He stated that constitutional morality is a natural sentiment present automatically in society.
3. He stated that it has to be cultivated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Ambedkar borrowed the term from George Grote and stated that constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment but one that has to be cultivated.
accepted.tq: Identify the negated definition in statement 2 and retain the precise formulation of the concept.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements expresses Ambedkar’s view of the relationship between political and social democracy?
o: Political democracy can survive independently of social and economic democracy.
Political democracy cannot last unless social and economic democracy form its foundation.
Social democracy is relevant only after economic development is complete.
Economic democracy is incompatible with constitutional government.
accepted.x: Ambedkar stated that political democracy cannot last unless social and economic democracy lie at its base.
accepted.tq: Select the precise relationship expressed in the constitutional speech rather than an absolute alternative.
accepted.sec: ■ Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

accepted.s: The Hindu Code Bill was primarily intended to provide Hindu women with equal rights in:
o: Employment, taxation, property registration and federal representation
Voting, citizenship, language and education only
Religious conversion, pilgrimage, temple administration and succession only
accepted.x: The Hindu Code Bill aimed at equal rights for Hindu women in inheritance, marriage, divorce and adoption.
accepted.tq: Choose the option covering all the stated subject areas of the Bill.
accepted.sec: ■ Hindu Code Bill - provisions and fate

accepted.s: The Hindu Code Bill was introduced in:
accepted.x: The Hindu Code Bill was introduced in 1947. Its delayed and diluted progress later contributed to Ambedkar’s resignation as Law Minister in 1951.
accepted.tq: Keep the introduction year distinct from the year of Ambedkar’s resignation and the later enactments.
accepted.sec: ■ Hindu Code Bill - provisions and fate

accepted.s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar resign as Law Minister in 1951?
o: The Drafting Committee was dissolved before the Constitution was enacted.
The Hindu Code Bill was stalled and diluted in Parliament.
The Constituent Assembly rejected universal adult suffrage.
The Government of India Act, 1935 was repealed.
accepted.x: The Hindu Code Bill was stalled and diluted in Parliament, and this situation led Ambedkar to resign as Law Minister in 1951.
accepted.tq: Connect the legislative obstruction with the ministerial resignation rather than with unrelated constitutional events.
accepted.sec: ■ Hindu Code Bill - provisions and fate

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding later enactments connected with the Hindu Code Bill?
accepted.x: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act was enacted in 1956, not 1957. The other three pairings are correct.
accepted.tq: Check the year in each legal enactment and identify the single altered date.
accepted.sec: ■ Hindu Code Bill - provisions and fate

accepted.s: Which of the following titles is associated with Dr. B.R. Ambedkar?
accepted.x: Ambedkar has been referred to as the ‘Modern Manu’, besides being called the Father or chief architect of the Indian Constitution and the Messenger of Dalits.
accepted.tq: Discriminate among historically associated titles rather than among constitutional offices.

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements about Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is correct?
o: His signature was the first on the Constitution and he received the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990.
He was the first Speaker of the Dominion Legislature and received the Bharat Ratna in 1950.
He signed the Constitution last and received the Bharat Ratna in 1975.
He was Constitutional Adviser and received the Bharat Ratna in 1995.
accepted.x: Ambedkar’s signature was the first on the Constitution, and he was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990.
accepted.tq: Combine two biographical facts while rejecting options that swap Ambedkar’s office with another office-bearer.

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Constitution Day is observed on 26 November.
2. Its observance began in 2015.
3. The year 2015 marked Ambedkar’s 125th birth anniversary.
4. Hindi Diwas is observed on 14 September.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All four statements are correct. Constitution Day is observed on 26 November since 2015, the year of Ambedkar’s 125th birth anniversary, while Hindi Diwas is observed on 14 September.
accepted.tq: Check the dates and the linked commemorative occasion without confusing Constitution Day with Hindi Diwas.

accepted.s: The Munshi-Ayyangar formula, associated with the constitutional language settlement, was adopted on:
accepted.x: The Munshi-Ayyangar formula was adopted on 14 September 1949. The date is also associated with the observance of Hindi Diwas on 14 September.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the language formula’s adoption date from the Constitution’s adoption date.

accepted.s: Which of the following combinations best represents the social revolution embedded in the constitutional framework associated with Ambedkar?
o: Rights, reservation and abolition of untouchability
Religious uniformity, economic isolation and military rule
Separate electorates, unrestricted executive power and censorship
Monarchy, hereditary privilege and provincial secession
accepted.x: The constitutional framework embedded a social revolution through rights, reservation and the abolition of untouchability.
accepted.tq: Identify the cluster of mutually reinforcing social-justice measures rather than isolated political arrangements.
